note: The fixed set of BEHAVIOUR checks. Read _checks/readme.md before adding one. Run: npm run check:behavior (from projects-app/).

cases.why: A greeting must not become work. It is the cheapest run there is, and it is also the run that proves the intent layer keeps small talk out of the middle.

Caught live in step 314: the automation wrote 'send me a weekly report' into its own standing instruction — a promise it cannot keep, and it would have repeated it to the model on every run afterwards. The check aims at the BEHAVIOUR INSTRUCTION, not at the whole core: the gap journal legitimately quotes the request in a warning to the owner, and forbidding that would forbid him ever learning what people ask for. MEASURED 2026-08-04: the coverage verdict on this very sentence is NOT stable — the same text was judged 'gap' twice and 'covered' once, which is the fragility of prose classification in one line. So the case asserts the law that does hold either way: whatever the verdict, an impossible promise must never reach the behaviour instruction.

cases.why: Same text as the case above, but picked from the list: coverage is KNOWN, not judged. Measured 2026-08-04, and it corrected the claim written the same morning — the run is not CHEAPER. `checkCoverage` shares one cached adjustment read with the evolution layer, which pays for it on these classes anyway, so the list buys exactness, not a saved call. Recorded here so the claim can never drift back.

cases.why: THE OWNER'S OWN SESSION, 2026-08-04, and the reason this case exists. He opened the page with the interface in Russian, typed 'hello' out of habit, and the automation locked the conversation to English forever — because the panel never told the run what language the page was in, and the run guessed from the alphabet of one word. A person reading a Russian page must be answered in Russian. Every case before this one was written in English through an English panel, which is exactly why eight green checks proved nothing about this.

THE OWNER'S OWN SESSION: he wrote 'i need only russian' and was told 'I don't do Russian yet, but I can help ... in English'. The honest-refusal rule — say plainly when something is not part of this build — was applied to LANGUAGE, which the build does have. That is the worst kind of refusal: the person leaves believing the machine cannot speak his language. Reproduced three times afterwards and it answered correctly each time, so the path is UNSTABLE, not dead — and unstable is worse for a user than broken, because it cannot be predicted. Hence a permanent case.

The abilities brief costs ~750 tokens, so 332.C sends it in full ONLY on the classes that talk about the build itself. This case guards the half that must not degrade: asked point blank, the automation still describes itself, in terms of what the person GETS. The forbidden words are the ones the node summaries are written in — the owner caught them being retold verbatim once (330.5R), and a shorter brief must not bring that back. MEASURED: the CLASS of 'what can you do?' is not stable — it comes back `self-describe` or `unclaimed` on the same text (second sighting of unstable prose classification today). Harmless here, because both classes receive the full brief, and the case therefore asserts the reply, not the verdict.
The only class that proves the whole chain end to end: input → intent → middle work → speech. If the middle stops being reached, everything else still looks green.

THE OWNER'S OWN SESSION: the flagship use case is 'I name a subject' — so a bare name, with no question mark and no polite framing, must run it. It did fetch, keep the picture and resolve the date, and then SPEECH lied: 'Понял: это напоминание на 01.01.1889' — because the summary called any date in the context a reminder, while the date belonged to the subject itself. The person asked for a landmark and was told about a reminder he never requested. The case asserts what he must see: the subject named back to him, and no reminder invented.

The order of layers, learned the hard way: anything that must be SAID has to happen before speech. A question raised after it is never delivered, and the person is left waiting for an answer that was never sent.

PROVEN DEFECT, then fixed (332.B). Hermes protects the first turns explicitly (protect_first_human); we protected only the last, so the opening — the turn that names the subject — was the first thing evicted. This case caught it live: 'the wedding is in <city>' → three turns of small talk → 'which city?' → 'I don't find that here, I only see the music note'. The session summary does NOT cover this: it is written when turns leave the BUFFER, and these turns never left it — they simply did not fit the READ budget, which had no condensation at all. The fix pins the first substantial turn of the person (`OPENING_MIN` / `OPENING_SHARE` in context.ts). The subject word is generated fresh on every run, so a pass can never come from the shared long memory.
